Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). A function $a\colon\mathbb N\to R$ has **finite support** when there is $N\in\mathbb N$ such that $a_i=0$ for every $i>N$. The **polynomial ring** $R[x]$ is the set of all finitely supported functions $a\colon\mathbb N\to R$.

For $a,b\in R[x]$ and $n\in\mathbb N$, define

$$ (a+b)_n:=a_n+b_n,\qquad (ab)_n:=\sum_{i+j=n}a_i b_j. $$

The convolution sum is a finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $R$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). Write $0$ for the zero sequence, $1$ for the sequence with coefficient $1_R$ at index $0$ and zero elsewhere, and $x$ for the sequence with coefficient $1_R$ at index $1$ and zero elsewhere. The coefficient sequence supported at $0$ with value $r$ is denoted again by $r$, and a polynomial $a$ is written formally as $\sum_i a_i x^i$.

The closure of these operations and the commutative-ring axioms are established by [[lem-polynomial-operations-preserve-finite-support]] and [[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]].

For every commutative ring $R$, the coefficientwise addition and convolution multiplication of [[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]] make $R[x]$ a commutative ring. The constant-polynomial map $c\colon R\to R[x]$ is an injective unital ring homomorphism ([[def-ring-homomorphism]]).

The ideal generated by a subset and principal ideals.

For $S\subseteq R$, define $(S)$ to be the intersection of all two-sided ideals
of $R$ containing $S$.  This family is nonempty because it contains $R$, and
[[lem-ideal-criterion-and-intersections]] shows that $(S)$ is an ideal.  For
$a\in R$, the ideal $(\{a\})$ is written $(a)$ and is called **principal**.

The quotient ring $R/I$ with $(r+I)(s+I)=rs+I$.

Let $I\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$.  Since $I$ is an additive subgroup of the
abelian group $(R,+)$, its additive cosets form the quotient group $R/I$
([[def-quotient-group]], [[cor-subgroups-of-abelian-groups-are-normal]]).  Define

$$(r+I)(s+I):=rs+I.$$

The well-definedness and ring laws are established by
[[thm-quotient-ring-multiplication-well-defined-iff-ideal]] and
[[thm-quotient-ring-laws]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $g\in R[x]$ be monic. For every $f\in R[x]$ there are unique $q,r\in R[x]$ such that

$$ f=qg+r,\qquad r=0\ \text{or}\ \deg r<\deg g. $$

This includes the zero dividend and a constant monic divisor.

derivations.claim: Let $Q=R[X]/(G)$. By [F1] and [F2], $R[X]$ is a commutative polynomial ring, and [F3] makes $(G)$ a two-sided ideal and $Q$ a quotient ring. Since $G$ is monic of degree two, [F4] gives every class in $Q$ a representative $a(p)+b(p)X$ of degree at most one in $X$. If two such representatives define the same class, their difference is a multiple of $G$ and has degree less than two; uniqueness in [F4] forces the difference to be zero. Thus this representative is unique.

Construct the coefficient-substitution homomorphism R[X] to Z[x,x^-1] explicitly; it kills G and therefore induces a map from Q. In Q, X(X-p)=1, so the explicit Laurent substitution x to X and x^-1 to X-p gives the inverse map. The composites fix x and the generators p,X of Q, so the maps are inverse; step 1.1 then transfers the unique degree-at-most-one representative to the unique Laurent decomposition.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\delta\in R$, and use the noncrossing-pairing diagram category of [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]], with the left factor stacked above the right factor. For a basis diagram $D:n\to n$, close each top endpoint to the corresponding bottom endpoint outside the rectangle and let $c(D)$ be the number of circles in the resulting finite graph. Define

$$\operatorname{Tr}_n(D)=\delta^{c(D)}$$

and extend $R$-linearly to $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$. This is the **unnormalized closure trace**. In particular, $\operatorname{Tr}_0(1_0)=1$ and $\operatorname{Tr}_n(1_n)=\delta^n$. No unit or nonzero condition on $\delta$ is required.

Let $\cup:0\to2$ and $\cap:2\to0$ be the standard cup and cap in the diagram category. For $n\ge1$ define the **right partial trace** by

$$\operatorname{ptr}_n(x)=(1_{n-1}\otimes\cap)\circ(x\otimes1_1)\circ(1_{n-1}\otimes\cup),\qquad x\in\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta).$$

It is a map $\mathrm{TL}_n\to\mathrm{TL}_{n-1}$. If $\delta$ is a unit, define $\tau_n=\delta^{-n}\operatorname{Tr}_n$. This agrees with the normalized trace of [[def-temperley-lieb-normalized-markov-trace-by-closure]] over $\mathbb C$ when $\delta\ne0$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and let $\delta\in R$. The object labels are the nonnegative integers $n=0,1,2,\ldots$. For labels $m,n$, place bottom points $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ and top points $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ along the rectangle from left to right on their respective edges. Their cyclic order is $t_1,\ldots,t_n,b_m,\ldots,b_1$. When $m=n=0$, the empty matching is included.

An $(m,n)$ **diagram** is a perfect matching of these $m+n$ boundary labels which is noncrossing: there are no four labels $a,b,c,d$ in cyclic order whose matched pairs are $\{a,c\}$ and $\{b,d\}$. A picture consists of disjoint arcs realizing the matching; equality is equality of the matching, so planar deformation that fixes the boundary does not change a diagram. If $m+n$ is odd, there are no such diagrams. Write $\mathcal D(m,n)$ for this set and define the $R$-module

$$M_R(m,n):=R^{(\mathcal D(m,n))},$$

the free $R$-module on the set of diagrams ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]). In particular, its diagram basis is empty when $m+n$ is odd.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]], with $h=\frac{1}{4(n+1)}$ and
$q_j=((2j-n-1)h,0)$. Fix an index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$. The two adjacent
base points are

$$q_i=\bigl((2i-n-1)h,0\bigr),\qquad q_{i+1}=\bigl((2i+1-n)h,0\bigr),$$

their **midpoint** is $m_i:=(q_i+q_{i+1})/2=((2i-n)h,0)=q_i+(h,0)$, and their
**support disc** is the open disc

$$U_i:=\bigl\{w\in\mathbb R^2:\lVert w-m_i\rVert_2<\tfrac32h\bigr\}.$$

The support disc contains the two base points $q_i,q_{i+1}$, whose distance from
$m_i$ is $h$, and it contains no other base point: for $k<i$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(i-k)+1)h\ge 3h$ and for $k>i+1$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(k-i)-1)h\ge3h$, both exceeding $\tfrac32h$. Moreover
$U_i\subseteq D^\circ$, because every point of $U_i$ has norm at most
$\lVert m_i\rVert_2+\tfrac32h\le(n-2)h+\tfrac32h<(n+1)h<1$. Finally
$U_i\cap U_j=\varnothing$ whenever $|i-j|>1$, since then the midpoints are at
distance $2|i-j|h\ge4h>3h$, twice the radius.

**The positive half twist.** Define $\rho\colon I\to\mathbb R^2$, the
**anticlockwise diamond path**, by

$$\rho(t):=\begin{cases}\bigl(2th-h,\,-2th\bigr),&0\le t\le \tfrac12,\\[2pt] \bigl(2th-h,\,2th-2h\bigr),&\tfrac12\le t\le1.\end{cases}$$

Thus $\rho(0)=(-h,0)$, $\rho(\tfrac12)=(0,-h)$, $\rho(1)=(h,0)$, and $\rho$ is
continuous, piecewise linear, and satisfies $\lVert\rho(t)\rVert_2\le h$ for all
$t$ with $\rho(t)\neq0$ throughout. The **elementary half twist at $i$**, written
$\sigma_i$, is the tuple of motions

$$(\sigma_i)_i(t):=m_i+\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_k(t):=q_k\ \ (k\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$

It is a braid based at $Q$
([[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]],
[[def-continuous-map-top]]): the two moving points stay in $U_i$ and are
antipodal about $m_i$, so they are distinct; every other point is fixed and lies
outside $U_i$; and the endpoint permutation is the transposition of $i$ and
$i+1$, since $(\sigma_i)_i(1)=m_i+(h,0)=q_{i+1}$ and
$(\sigma_i)_{i+1}(1)=m_i-(h,0)=q_i$.

The words *positive* and *anticlockwise* refer to the fixed orientation of the
plane of the disc and to the fixed planar projection whose horizontal axis
contains $Q$: the moving pair turns through the half turn anticlockwise, the
label $i$ passing below its midpoint and the label $i+1$ above. Together with
the first-under-second stacking convention of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]] this fixes the sign
convention for every signed crossing on this page and its companion.

**The opposite half twist.** The **opposite** (clockwise) half twist at $i$ is
defined by the reflected path

$$\rho^{-}(t):=\bigl(\rho_1(t),-\rho_2(t)\bigr),$$

through the motions $(\sigma_i^{-})_i(t):=m_i+\rho^{-}(t)$,
$(\sigma_i^{-})_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho^{-}(t)$ and
$(\sigma_i^{-})_k(t):=q_k$ for $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$. It is again a braid supported
in $U_i$ with endpoint permutation the transposition of $i$ and $i+1$; its pair
turns through the same half turn clockwise, the label $i$ passing above the
midpoint. The two motions are not equal, and they are not related by a
reparametrisation of the height: they are the two signed crossings of the pair.

**The opposite motion is the group inverse.** For a braid $\beta$ the reversed
braid $\overline\beta_j(t)=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)$ represents
$[\beta]^{-1}$ in the group $G_n$
([[thm-geometric-braids-form-a-group]]). For $\beta=\sigma_i$ one computes
$\overline{\sigma_i}=\sigma_i^{-}$: reversing the height and relabelling by the
transposition of $i$ and $i+1$ sends $\rho(t)=m_i+(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ to the
motion with relative path $-\rho(1-t)$, which is the reflected path
$\rho^-$ traversed from $t=0$ to $t=1$. Hence

$$[\sigma_i^{-}]=[\sigma_i]^{-1}\qquad\text{in }G_n .$$

**Elementary cases.** For $n\le1$ there is no index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$,
and there are no elementary half twists; the assertions above are vacuous. For
$n\ge2$ and $1\le i\le n-1$ both $[\sigma_i]$ and $[\sigma_i^{-}]$ are
nonidentity elements of $G_n$, since their endpoint permutations are
transpositions, which are not the identity permutation.

**Two letters do not commute in general.** For adjacent indices the supports
$U_i$ and $U_{i+1}$ overlap and no commutation is asserted;
[[lem-geometric-far-commutativity]] proves commutativity only for disjoint
supports.

and the distinct strands at that height have distinct disk coordinates;
at integral heights only the specified adjacent endpoints agree.
Thus each cycle gives an embedded circle. Different cycles give

$\{(\sqrt{1-q_j^2}e^{2\pi it},q_j):[t]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\}$.

oriented $3$-sphere, after moving the link off the point at infinity. Fix the
unit viewing normal $n$ pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ by the rule that

basis of the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, let $v_{\rm over}$ and
$v_{\rm under}$ be the nonzero projected tangent vectors following the
orientations of the overpassing and underpassing strands. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c):=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})\in\{+1,-1\}.$$

the braid chart $(x,y,t)$ with ambient orientation $(x,y,t)$, view along $+y$;
the induced positive orientation of the $(x,t)$ projection plane is the ordered
basis $(\partial_t,\partial_x)$. For the positive half twist, label $i$ moves
from $x=-h$ to $x=h$ below the midpoint, while label $i+1$ moves from $x=h$ to
$x=-h$ above it, with $h>0$. Thus the over and under projected tangent vectors
in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is

$$\operatorname{wr}(D):=\sum_{c\text{ a crossing of }D}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$

vanishes; it is perpendicular to the projected tangent, hence also to the
spatial tangent, and therefore represents a nonzero normal section of the

Assume full AC for the library Jones invariant. An oriented link is a finite
disjoint union of oriented smooth circles embedded in $S^3$, considered up to
ambient isotopy; an oriented classical knot is the one-component case. For a nonempty
oriented link $L\subset S^3$, let $V_L(x)\in\mathbb Z[x^{\pm1}]$ be the
library-normalized Jones polynomial, with $V_U(x)=1$ for the unknot $U$;
write $V_K$ for its value on a knot $K$. Here $x=t^{1/2}$ in the library
convention $t=A^{-4}$, so an oriented skein triple satisfies
$$x^{-2}V_{L_+}(x)-x^2V_{L_-}(x)=(x-x^{-1})V_{L_0}(x).$$
Set $p=x-x^{-1}$. By the unique Laurent decomposition, write
$$V_K(x)=\sum_{q\ge0}(a_q(K)+b_q(K)x)p^q,$$
where $a_q(K),b_q(K)\in\mathbb Z$ and only finitely many are nonzero. The
**Jones–Vassiliev coefficient vector of order $q$** is
$$f_q(K):=(a_q(K),b_q(K))^{\mathsf T},$$
and $c_q(K):=a_q(K)+b_q(K)$. This is the algebraic coefficient-vector
definition used by Carmi and Cohen. The claim that the coordinates of $f_q$
are finite-type invariants of order at most $q$ is a separate theorem and is
not part of this definition.

Let $x$ be an invertible indeterminate and put $p=x-x^{-1}$. Every Laurent
polynomial $P(x)\in\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]$ has a unique expression
$$P(x)=a(p)+b(p)x$$
with $a,b\in\mathbb Z[p]$, where $\mathbb Z[p]$ is the ring of finite

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be an unoriented link type in $S^3$. Its **crossing number** $c(K)$ is the least element of
$$\{\,n\in\mathbb N:\text{some regular diagram of }K\text{ has exactly }n\text{ crossings}\,\}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

citations.quote:
Assume full AC for the library Jones invariant. An oriented link is a finite
disjoint union of oriented smooth circles embedded in $S^3$, considered up to
ambient isotopy; an oriented classical knot is the one-component case. For a nonempty
oriented link $L\subset S^3$, let $V_L(x)\in\mathbb Z[x^{\pm1}]$ be the
library-normalized Jones polynomial, with $V_U(x)=1$ for the unknot $U$;
write $V_K$ for its value on a knot $K$. Here $x=t^{1/2}$ in the library
convention $t=A^{-4}$, so an oriented skein triple satisfies
$$x^{-2}V_{L_+}(x)-x^2V_{L_-}(x)=(x-x^{-1})V_{L_0}(x).$$
Set $p=x-x^{-1}$. By the unique Laurent decomposition, write
$$V_K(x)=\sum_{q\ge0}(a_q(K)+b_q(K)x)p^q,$$
where $a_q(K),b_q(K)\in\mathbb Z$ and only finitely many are nonzero. The
**Jones–Vassiliev coefficient vector of order $q$** is
$$f_q(K):=(a_q(K),b_q(K))^{\mathsf T},$$
and $c_q(K):=a_q(K)+b_q(K)$. This is the algebraic coefficient-vector
definition used by Carmi and Cohen. The claim that the coordinates of $f_q$
are finite-type invariants of order at most $q$ is a separate theorem and is
not part of this definition.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be an unoriented link type in $S^3$. Its **crossing number** $c(K)$ is the least element of
$$\{\,n\in\mathbb N:\text{some regular diagram of }K\text{ has exactly }n\text{ crossings}\,\}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
